title: The common good (CCC 1905–1912)

lines: A CROSSWALK, A LIBRARY, A BUS.
cards: A streetlight at the corner. Nobody owns it. Nobody thanks it.
But a nurse walking home from a late shift can see the curb, a kid finds the way back from a friend's house, and an old man takes his dog out without tripping.

Next to it: a crosswalk, a park fountain, a library with its doors open, a bus that runs on time. None of these makes anyone happy, exactly. They make it possible for many different people to get on with their lives.
When one goes dark, everyone feels it.

teach.h: THE GOOD OF EACH, BOUND TO ALL.
teach.b: The Catechism calls that whole web the common good. Because people are social by nature, it says, the good of each person is bound up with the good of all.

teach.h: CONDITIONS, NOT A SCRIPT FOR HAPPINESS.
teach.b: Its definition, borrowed from the Second Vatican Council: the sum of the social conditions that allow people, as groups and as individuals, to reach their fulfillment more fully and more easily.

Notice the word conditions. The common good isn't a society deciding what will make each person happy. It's the streetlight, not the walk home: it makes flourishing possible, and leaves the living to the people.
The Catechism names three essential parts.

First, respect for the person: public authorities must respect basic human rights, including the freedom to act by a sound conscience, the protection of privacy, and rightful freedom in matters of religion.

Second, social well-being and development: what a truly human life needs should be within reach, food, clothing, health, work, education and culture, suitable information, the right to start a family.
Third, peace: the stability and security of a just order. Then it widens the circle.
The human family is one, so there's also a universal common good, reaching across borders; it names refugees and migrants, and migrants' families.

And it ends with a reminder that keeps the idea honest: the order of society must serve the good of persons, not the other way around. It quotes Jesus in Mark: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath."

how: The common good is a central idea of Catholic social teaching, and the Church's documents invoke it when they speak about work, charity, civic life and politics.

games.q: you sit on a neighborhood board. an empty lot can become parking reserved for the board's own shops, a small park open to everyone, or stay fenced off. which fits the common good as the Catechism describes it?
o: a small park open to everyone.
leave it fenced; no one loses.
games.why: the common good is conditions that let everyone flourish, not the good of a few, and not nothing at all.

practice: Walk in your mind through the places you'll pass today, a sidewalk, an office kitchen, a group chat, and look for one thing that belongs to nobody, serves everybody, and could use a hand: litter by a bench, a broken light to report, a sink of shared mugs, a newcomer nobody has greeted.
Picture yourself doing it, without anyone noticing. If you pray, offer it for the people who'll never know.

wordCard.voice: Common good. The social conditions that let people, together and one by one, reach their fulfillment more fully and more easily: respect for the person, well-being, and peace. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the common good — the phrase used in Catholic social teaching.
